  3. bigint: arbitrary-precision integers for the JavaScript engine

#bigint: arbitrary-precision integers for the JavaScript engine

src/engine/bigint is the ECMAScript BigInt arithmetic, written natively in Odin. The JavaScript engine used to get this from QuickJS's C running inside WebAssembly; this package replaces it with a native implementation that gives identical numeric results and reads like Odin instead of transcribed C.

It is allocation-aware: every operation allocates its result through context.allocator, so the engine injects the realm's allocator and frees results with destroy. No OS dependency — it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32.

#Representation

Sign-magnitude, little-endian u32 limbs, always normalized (no leading zero limb; zero is the empty magnitude with neg = false). This is the natural Odin shape and keeps the arithmetic obvious. The one place the choice shows is the bitwise operators: ECMAScript defines & | ^ ~ and >> as if a BigInt were an infinite two's-complement integer, so those operations convert each operand to its two's-complement limb view over a common width, apply the op, and convert back (bits.odin).

Odin
import bi "wb:engine/bigint"

a := bi.from_i64(1_000_000_007)
b, _ := bi.from_string("340282366920938463463374607431768211456", 10) // 2^128
defer bi.destroy(&a)
defer bi.destroy(&b)

p := bi.mul(a, b);            defer bi.destroy(&p)
q := bi.div(p, a);            defer bi.destroy(&q)   // == b
s := bi.to_string(q, 16);     defer delete(s)        // "100000000000000000000000000000000"
d := bi.to_f64(b)                                     // 3.402823669209385e+38
m := bi.as_uintn(32, a);      defer bi.destroy(&m)   // BigInt.asUintN(32, a)

#Operations

  • Arithmetic: add, sub, neg, abs, mul, div, rem, divmod, pow.
  • Comparison: cmp (-1/0/1), equals, sign, is_zero.
  • Shifts: shl, shr (arithmetic — a >> n == floor(a / 2ⁿ), so it sign-extends negatives).
  • Bitwise: bit_and, bit_or, bit_xor, bit_not, with two's-complement semantics.
  • Width wrap: as_intn(bits, a), as_uintn(bits, a).
  • Conversion: from_i64, from_u64, from_f64, to_f64 (round-to-nearest-ties-to-even), from_string/to_string in any base 2–36.

Multiplication is schoolbook below ~40 limbs and Karatsuba above it; division is Knuth's Algorithm D (with a single-limb fast path). String conversion packs as many base-R digits as fit in a u32 before each big multiply/divide, so parsing or printing a very large number stays close to linear.

#How we know it is correct

There is no small C oracle for BigInt (the QuickJS version needs the whole engine, and no Python was available), so a differential judge pins correctness two ways over 12,000,000+ checks:

  1. Exact agreement with native i128/u128 for operands in that range — add, sub, mul, div, rem, all the bit ops, shifts, asIntN/asUintN, and decimal matches %d — plus string round trips in every base 2–36.
  2. Algebraic identities for large operands (up to several thousand bits, well into the Karatsuba path): (a+b)-b == a, (a*b)/b == a, (a/b)*b + a%b == a with sign(rem) == sign(a), to_string/from_string round trips, (a<<n)>>n == a, pow versus repeated multiply, and from_f64(to_f64(a)) == a for integers exactly representable in f64.

Result: 0 failures.

#Integration

Division by zero and a negative exponent are RangeErrors in ECMAScript; the engine must reject them before calling div/rem/pow (the package returns zero rather than trapping, to stay allocation-safe). BigInt(string) strips the 0x/0o/0b prefix and separators and calls from_string; BigInt(number) checks integrality then calls from_f64; Number(bigint) calls to_f64; toString(radix) calls to_string.
